claim: P. aeruginosa can modify surface motility in response to secreted factors from S. aureus.
source: By imaging two prevalent pathogens known to be coisolated from chronic illnesses, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, we observed P. aeruginosa can modify surface motility in response to secreted factors from S. aureus.
evidence: Supported by live-imaging experiments showing P. aeruginosa behavioral changes in the presence of S. aureus

claim: Upon sensing S. aureus, P. aeruginosa transitioned from collective to single-cell motility with an associated increase in speed and directedness.
source: Upon sensing S. aureus, P. aeruginosa transitioned from collective to single-cell motility with an associated increase in speed and directedness – a behavior we refer to as 'exploratory motility'.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing changes in P. aeruginosa motility patterns

claim: Explorer cells moved preferentially towards S. aureus.
source: Explorer cells moved preferentially towards S. aureus and invaded S. aureus colonies through the action of the type IV pili.
evidence: Supported by live-imaging observations and tracking data

claim: P. aeruginosa invaded S. aureus colonies through the action of the type IV pili.
source: Explorer cells moved preferentially towards S. aureus and invaded S. aureus colonies through the action of the type IV pili.
evidence: Supported by experiments with pilA mutants showing loss of invasion behavior

claim: Coisolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus from the CF airway or chronic wounds is associated with poor patient outcomes, including decreased lung function and shortened life-spans.
source: For example, we and others find an association between coisolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus from the CF airway or chronic wounds and poor patient outcomes, including decreased lung function and shortened life-spans (Limoli et al., 2016; Maliniak et al., 2016; Hubert et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Interactions between P. aeruginosa and S. aureus can alter virulence factor production by one or both species.
source: Laboratory studies also reveal interactions between these two pathogens can alter virulence factor production by one or both species, potentially influencing pathogenesis, persistence, and/or antibiotic susceptibility (Hotterbeekx et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review

claim: P. aeruginosa and S. aureus form mixed microcolonies in a model of coinfection on CF-derived bronchial epithelial cells.
source: For example, in a model of coinfection on CF-derived bronchial epithelial cells, we observed P. aeruginosa and S. aureus form mixed microcolonies, which promotes the survival of S. aureus in the presence of vancomycin (Orazi and O'Toole, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Mixed microcolonies of P. aeruginosa and S. aureus promote the survival of S. aureus in the presence of vancomycin.
source: For example, in a model of coinfection on CF-derived bronchial epithelial cells, we observed P. aeruginosa and S. aureus form mixed microcolonies, which promotes the survival of S. aureus in the presence of vancomycin (Orazi and O'Toole, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: P. aeruginosa cells replicate and expand outward as raft-like groups when grown alone.
source: Alone, P. aeruginosa cells replicate and expand outward as raft-like groups, as previously described for P. aeruginosa surface-based motility (Anyan et al., 2014; Burrows, 2012) (Video 1; Figure 1, still montage, top row).
evidence: Supported by live-imaging data and citations to previous descriptions

claim: Coincubation with S. aureus resulted in dramatically altered P. aeruginosa behavior compared to monoculture.
source: In comparison, coincubation with S. aureus resulted in dramatically altered behavior (Video 2, Figure 1, still montage, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by comparison of Videos 1 and 2 and Figure 1

claim: After two to three rounds of cell division in the presence of S. aureus, individual P. aeruginosa cells began to increase motility and moved as single-cells.
source: After two to three rounds of cell division, instead of remaining as a group, individual P. aeruginosa cells began to increase motility and moved as single-cells, suggesting that P. aeruginosa responds to the presence of S. aureus by altering motility behaviors.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging observations

claim: P. aeruginosa significantly inhibited S. aureus growth.
source: P. aeruginosa significantly inhibited S. aureus growth, as previously reported (see Figure 1—video 1 for representative time-lapse video of S. aureus alone).
evidence: Supported by comparison of S. aureus growth in monoculture versus coculture

claim: P. aeruginosa cells exited the raft when the community approached S. aureus.
source: P. aeruginosa cells initially replicated and remained in a raft (t = 4 h:28 m), as we and others have observed for P. aeruginosa in monoculture, but as the community approached S. aureus, individual cells: (1) exited the raft (t = 4 h:34 m)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging at specified time points

claim: P. aeruginosa cells moved with increased speed when approaching S. aureus.
source: P. aeruginosa cells initially replicated and remained in a raft (t = 4 h:28 m), as we and others have observed for P. aeruginosa in monoculture, but as the community approached S. aureus, individual cells: (1) exited the raft (t = 4 h:34 m), (2) moved with increased speed
evidence: Supported by quantitative tracking data shown in Figure 2E

claim: P. aeruginosa cells moved towards and surrounded S. aureus, exploring the surface of the colony.
source: and (3) moved towards and surrounded S. aureus, 'explored' the surface of the colony until (Figure 2A–B)
evidence: Supported by live-imaging observations in Figure 2A-B

claim: P. aeruginosa cells entered the S. aureus colony by 6 hours.
source: (4) P. aeruginosa cells entered the S. aureus colony (Figure 2C, t = 6 hr)
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging at 6 hours showing P. aeruginosa inside S. aureus colonies

claim: By 8 hours, P. aeruginosa completely dismantled the S. aureus community.
source: and finally, (5) by 8 hr, P. aeruginosa completely dismantled the S. aureus community (Figure 2D, t = 8 hr).
evidence: Supported by imaging at 8 hours showing disrupted S. aureus colonies

claim: P. aeruginosa adopted a swift motion beginning between 4.5-6 hours, moving in and out of the plane of focus during imaging.
source: P. aeruginosa was also observed to adopt a swift motion, beginning between 4.5–6 hr, moving in and out of the plane of focus during imaging (Video 4, yellow circle and Figure 2D, red arrows).
evidence: Supported by Video 4 and Figure 2D showing cells moving out of focus

claim: Individual P. aeruginosa cells moved with increased speed compared to cells moving in rafts.
source: In comparison to cells moving in rafts, individual cells moved with increased speed (µm/s), acceleration (µm/s2), and mean squared displacement (MSD, µm2) (Figure 2E, F and G, respectively).
evidence: Supported by quantitative tracking data in Figure 2E-G

claim: Individual P. aeruginosa cells moved with increased acceleration compared to cells moving in rafts.
source: In comparison to cells moving in rafts, individual cells moved with increased speed (µm/s), acceleration (µm/s2), and mean squared displacement (MSD, µm2) (Figure 2E, F and G, respectively).
evidence: Supported by quantitative tracking data in Figure 2E-G

claim: Individual P. aeruginosa cells moved with increased mean squared displacement compared to cells moving in rafts.
source: In comparison to cells moving in rafts, individual cells moved with increased speed (µm/s), acceleration (µm/s2), and mean squared displacement (MSD, µm2) (Figure 2E, F and G, respectively).
evidence: Supported by quantitative tracking data in Figure 2E-G

claim: Increased MSD in single P. aeruginosa cells suggests they exhibit directed motion.
source: MSD represents a combined measure of both the speed and directional persistence of the cell, thus an increased MSD in single-cells over a change in time suggests single-cells exhibit directed motion, followed by a decreased MSD when P. aeruginosa cells reach the S. aureus colony.
evidence: Based on interpretation of MSD measurements from tracking data

claim: P. aeruginosa performs cellular movement through the action of a single polar flagellum and the type IV pili when grown in monoculture.
source: When grown in monoculture, P. aeruginosa performs cellular movement through the action of a single polar flagellum and the type IV pili (TFP) (Conrad et al., 2011; Gibiansky et al., 2010; Merritt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The ΔpilA mutant was unable to move away from the group as single-cells.
source: The ΔpilA mutant was unable to move away from the group as single-cells (Video 5), as seen for the parental P. aeruginosa (Video 4), suggesting the TFP are required for P. aeruginosa exploratory motility.
evidence: Supported by comparison of Videos 4 and 5 showing different behaviors

claim: TFP are required for P. aeruginosa exploratory motility.
source: The ΔpilA mutant was unable to move away from the group as single-cells (Video 5), as seen for the parental P. aeruginosa (Video 4), suggesting the TFP are required for P. aeruginosa exploratory motility.
evidence: Inferred from the inability of ΔpilA mutant to perform single-cell motility

claim: The swift movement observed in wild-type P. aeruginosa was maintained in ΔpilA.
source: However, the swift movement observed in the WT (Figure 3A, see boxed inset with red arrows), was maintained in ΔpilA, demonstrating that TFP are not required for this behavior.
evidence: Supported by imaging showing swift movement in ΔpilA mutant

claim: TFP are not required for swift movement behavior in P. aeruginosa.
source: However, the swift movement observed in the WT (Figure 3A, see boxed inset with red arrows), was maintained in ΔpilA, demonstrating that TFP are not required for this behavior.
evidence: Demonstrated by retention of swift movement in ΔpilA mutant

claim: The ΔflgK mutant adopted the single-cell behaviors of the wild-type.
source: We next examined the ΔflgK mutant (Figure 3—video 1), which was seen to adopt the single-cell behaviors of the WT, except the swift movements were not observed
evidence: Supported by live-imaging of ΔflgK mutant

claim: Swift movements were not observed in the ΔflgK mutant.
source: We next examined the ΔflgK mutant (Figure 3—video 1), which was seen to adopt the single-cell behaviors of the WT, except the swift movements were not observed, supporting the hypothesis that this movement is generated by the flagellum.
evidence: Supported by live-imaging showing absence of swift movement in ΔflgK

claim: Swift movement is generated by the flagellum.
source: We next examined the ΔflgK mutant (Figure 3—video 1), which was seen to adopt the single-cell behaviors of the WT, except the swift movements were not observed, supporting the hypothesis that this movement is generated by the flagellum.
evidence: Inferred from loss of swift movement in flagella-deficient mutant

claim: S. aureus modulates both TFP and flagella-mediated motility in P. aeruginosa.
source: These data suggest that while S. aureus modulates both TFP and flagella-mediated motility, the early events necessary for exploration (initiation of single-cell movement and directional movement towards S. aureus) require the TFP.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects on ΔpilA and ΔflgK mutants

claim: The early events necessary for exploration (initiation of single-cell movement and directional movement towards S. aureus) require the TFP.
source: These data suggest that while S. aureus modulates both TFP and flagella-mediated motility, the early events necessary for exploration (initiation of single-cell movement and directional movement towards S. aureus) require the TFP.
evidence: Inferred from requirement of pilA for single-cell motility and directional movement

claim: P. aeruginosa cells deficient in both TFP and flagella were unable to remain within a raft-like group.
source: P. aeruginosa cells deficient in both TFP and flagella were not only unable to produce the respective movements characteristic of these motility motors, but also were unable to remain within a raft-like group (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by imaging of ΔpilA ΔflgK double mutant

claim: The dispersed behavior of ΔpilA ΔflgK was not dependent upon the presence of S. aureus.
source: This behavior was not dependent upon the presence of S. aureus, as a similar pattern was observed for ΔpilA ΔflgK when visualized in the absence of S. aureus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging of ΔpilA ΔflgK in monoculture

claim: S. aureus colonies were significantly smaller in the presence of WT P. aeruginosa or the ΔflgK mutant in comparison to S. aureus grown in monoculture.
source: S. aureus colonies were significantly smaller in the presence of WT P. aeruginosa or the ΔflgK mutant in comparison to S. aureus grown in monoculture (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of S. aureus colony area

claim: In the presence of the ΔpilA mutant, S. aureus colonies were significantly larger in comparison to WT and the ΔflgK mutant.
source: However, in the presence the ΔpilA mutant, which was deficient in exploratory motility, colonies were significantly larger in comparison to WT and the ΔflgK mutant.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of S. aureus colony area

claim: When grown in the presence of the ΔpilA ΔflgK double mutant, the area of the S. aureus colonies was not significantly different from S. aureus monoculture.
source: Moreover, when grown in the presence of the double mutant, the area of the S. aureus colonies was not significantly different from S. aureus monoculture.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of S. aureus colony area

claim: The ability of P. aeruginosa to perform exploratory motility influences P. aeruginosa inhibition of S. aureus growth.
source: These data suggest that ability of P. aeruginosa to perform exploratory motility influences P. aeruginosa inhibition of S. aureus growth.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between exploratory motility capability and S. aureus colony size

claim: When P. aeruginosa first encounters the S. aureus colony, the cell body orients perpendicular to the surface of the colony and moves back-and-forth.
source: When P. aeruginosa first encounters the S. aureus colony, the cell body orients perpendicular to the surface of the colony and moves back-and-forth (Video 4, blue circle and Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by high-speed imaging observations

claim: The back-and-forth motion appears to move P. aeruginosa cells into the S. aureus colony.
source: When P. aeruginosa first encounters the S. aureus colony, the cell body orients perpendicular to the surface of the colony and moves back-and-forth (Video 4, blue circle and Figure 3C) and appears to move P. aeruginosa cells into the S. aureus colony.
evidence: Based on observation of cell behavior at colony interface

claim: The back-and-forth behavior was only observed in the WT and ΔflgK mutant, suggesting that it is driven by the TFP.
source: This behavior was only observed in the WT and ΔflgK mutant, suggesting that it is driven by the TFP.
evidence: Inferred from presence in WT and ΔflgK but absence in ΔpilA

claim: P. aeruginosa responds to S. aureus secreted factors.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that P. aeruginosa responds to S. aureus secreted factors.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observation of distance-dependent response

claim: S. aureus supernatant significantly increased the motility diameter of P. aeruginosa in a dose-dependent manner.
source: S. aureus supernatant significantly increased the motility diameter of P. aeruginosa in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4A), supporting the hypothesis that S. aureus secreted factors increase P. aeruginosa twitching motility.
evidence: Supported by macroscopic twitching motility assay data

claim: S. aureus secreted factors increase P. aeruginosa twitching motility.
source: S. aureus supernatant significantly increased the motility diameter of P. aeruginosa in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4A), supporting the hypothesis that S. aureus secreted factors increase P. aeruginosa twitching motility.
evidence: Supported by dose-dependent increase in motility with S. aureus supernatant

claim: The sigB::Tn strain phenocopied the wild-type S. aureus in its ability to induce P. aeruginosa twitching motility.
source: While the sigB::Tn strain phenocopied the WT, the agrB::Tn mutant lost all ability to induce P. aeruginosa twitching motility, suggesting that Agr regulates the production of the factors promoting motility in P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assay with sigB mutant supernatant

claim: The agrB::Tn mutant lost all ability to induce P. aeruginosa twitching motility.
source: While the sigB::Tn strain phenocopied the WT, the agrB::Tn mutant lost all ability to induce P. aeruginosa twitching motility, suggesting that Agr regulates the production of the factors promoting motility in P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assay with agrB mutant supernatant

claim: Agr regulates the production of the factors promoting motility in P. aeruginosa.
source: While the sigB::Tn strain phenocopied the WT, the agrB::Tn mutant lost all ability to induce P. aeruginosa twitching motility, suggesting that Agr regulates the production of the factors promoting motility in P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Inferred from loss of activity in agrB mutant

claim: The ΔagrBDCA mutant was unable to enhance P. aeruginosa motility.
source: As predicted, the ΔagrBDCA mutant was unable to enhance P. aeruginosa motility, and complementation restored activity to WT levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assay with clean deletion mutant

claim: Complementation of ΔagrBDCA restored activity to wild-type levels.
source: As predicted, the ΔagrBDCA mutant was unable to enhance P. aeruginosa motility, and complementation restored activity to WT levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assay with complemented strain

claim: The ΔpilA mutant was unable to perform twitching motility in the absence of S. aureus supernatant.
source: In the absence of S. aureus supernatant, the ΔpilA mutant was unable to perform twitching motility, as previously reported (Darzins, 1994).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assay and citation to previous report

claim: The ΔpilA mutant retained some ability to respond to S. aureus secreted factors in the presence of supernatant.
source: However, while motility was reduced in the presence of S. aureus supernatant, surprisingly, the ΔpilA mutant retained some ability to respond to S. aureus secreted factors (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assay showing residual motility in ΔpilA with supernatant

claim: S. aureus can increase P. aeruginosa flagella-mediated motility in addition to TFP-mediated motility.
source: Since we observed during live-imaging that S. aureus can increase P. aeruginosa flagella-mediated motility, in addition to TFP-mediated motility, we hypothesized that the response retained in the ΔpilA mutant was due to increased flagella-mediated motility.
evidence: Hypothesis based on live-imaging observations and residual motility in ΔpilA

claim: The motility of the ΔpilA ΔflgK mutant was reduced to levels not significantly different from ΔpilA or ΔpilA ΔflgK in the absence of supernatant.
source: The single ΔflgK mutant phenotype trended lower, but was not significantly different from WT, while the motility of the ΔpilA ΔflgK mutant was reduced to levels not significantly different from ΔpilA or ΔpilA ΔflgK in the absence of supernatant (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative motility measurements

claim: TFP are the primary contributors to increased motility in response to S. aureus, but S. aureus secreted factors can increase both TFP- and flagella-mediated motility.
source: These data support our observation from live-imaging that, while TFP were the primary contributors to increased motility, S. aureus secreted factors could increase both TFP- and flagella-mediated motility.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects on single and double mutants

claim: The diameter of the P. aeruginosa motility zone showed a modest, but not significant increase in the presence of S. aureus supernatant in 0.3% agar swim assays.
source: The diameter of the P. aeruginosa motility zone showed a modest, but not significant increase in the presence of S. aureus supernatant, compared to medium alone (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by swim assay measurements

claim: Flagella-mediated motility was significantly reduced in the ΔflgK mutant both with and without S. aureus supernatant.
source: As expected, flagella-mediated motility, both with and without S. aureus supernatant, was significantly reduced.
evidence: Supported by swim assay with ΔflgK mutant

claim: The motility diameter of ΔpilA was not significantly different from WT in swim assays.
source: The motility diameter of ΔpilA was not significantly different from WT, and the double mutant phenocopied the single ΔflgK mutant, suggesting that flagella are primarily responsible for the motility observed here.
evidence: Supported by swim assay measurements

claim: Flagella are primarily responsible for the motility observed in 0.3% agar swim assays.
source: The motility diameter of ΔpilA was not significantly different from WT, and the double mutant phenocopied the single ΔflgK mutant, suggesting that flagella are primarily responsible for the motility observed here.
evidence: Inferred from similarity of ΔpilA to WT and double mutant to ΔflgK

claim: P. aeruginosa exhibited preferential movement towards supernatant derived from WT S. aureus.
source: Preferential movement of P. aeruginosa towards supernatant derived from WT S. aureus was observed, but not for medium alone or supernatant derived from the ΔagrBDCA mutant (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by directional twitching motility assay

claim: P. aeruginosa did not show preferential movement towards medium alone or supernatant derived from the ΔagrBDCA mutant.
source: Preferential movement of P. aeruginosa towards supernatant derived from WT S. aureus was observed, but not for medium alone or supernatant derived from the ΔagrBDCA mutant (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by directional twitching motility assay

claim: All motility was abrogated in the ΔpilA mutant in the directional twitching assay.
source: The response for the ΔpilA mutant was also examined and all motility was abrogated in this mutant, demonstrating motility observed in this assay is entirely pili-mediated.
evidence: Supported by directional twitching motility assay with ΔpilA

claim: Motility observed in the directional twitching assay is entirely pili-mediated.
source: The response for the ΔpilA mutant was also examined and all motility was abrogated in this mutant, demonstrating motility observed in this assay is entirely pili-mediated.
evidence: Demonstrated by complete loss of motility in ΔpilA mutant

claim: P. aeruginosa biases the directionality of TFP-mediated motility up a concentration gradient of S. aureus secreted factors.
source: These data support the hypothesis that P. aeruginosa biases the directionality of TFP-mediated motility up a concentration gradient of S. aureus secreted factors.
evidence: Supported by directional twitching assay results

claim: P. aeruginosa remained capable of initiating single-cell movement in the presence of ΔagrBDCA.
source: P. aeruginosa remained capable of initiating single-cell movement; however, once cells initiated single-cell movement, the path of their movement did not appear as directed towards the S. aureus colonies.
evidence: Supported by live-imaging with ΔagrBDCA mutant

claim: The path of P. aeruginosa movement did not appear as directed towards the ΔagrBDCA S. aureus colonies.
source: P. aeruginosa remained capable of initiating single-cell movement; however, once cells initiated single-cell movement, the path of their movement did not appear as directed towards the S. aureus colonies.
evidence: Supported by live-imaging observations and tracking

claim: Some P. aeruginosa cells seemed to actively avoid the ΔagrBDCA S. aureus colony.
source: In fact, some cells seemed to actively avoid the S. aureus colony all together.
evidence: Based on observation of cell trajectories in live-imaging

claim: P. aeruginosa exhibited a significantly higher directedness ratio towards WT S. aureus compared to the ΔagrBDCA mutant.
source: P. aeruginosa exhibited a significantly higher directedness ratio towards WT S. aureus compared to the ΔagrBDCA mutant (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of cell tracking data

claim: Agr regulates the production of S. aureus secreted factors driving the directionality of P. aeruginosa motility.
source: These data support the hypothesis that Agr regulates the production of S. aureus secreted factors driving the directionality of P. aeruginosa motility.
evidence: Supported by differential directedness towards WT versus ΔagrBDCA

claim: P. aeruginosa encodes three known chemotaxis pathways: two flagella-mediated (che and che2) and a putative TFP-mediated system (pil-chp).
source: P. aeruginosa encodes three known chemotaxis pathways: two flagella-mediated (che and che2) and a putative TFP-mediated system (pil-chp) (Darzins, 1994; Whitchurch et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Many proteins in the Pil-Chp pathway are required for pilus assembly.
source: A significant challenge lies in that many of these proteins are required for pilus assembly, thus teasing apart their requirement for motility per se versus regulation of a chemotactic response is challenging.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Pil-Chp pathway components

claim: PilJ is predicted to encode the TFP methyl-accepting chemoreceptor protein (MCP).
source: Nonetheless, pilJ is predicted to encode the TFP methyl-accepting chemoreceptor protein (MCP) and by homology to the flagella MCPs, PilJ is expected to detect changes in the concentration of an attractant or repellent and initiate a signaling cascade to control twitching motility.
evidence: Based on sequence homology and predicted function

claim: PilJ is expected to detect changes in the concentration of an attractant or repellent and initiate a signaling cascade to control twitching motility.
source: Nonetheless, pilJ is predicted to encode the TFP methyl-accepting chemoreceptor protein (MCP) and by homology to the flagella MCPs, PilJ is expected to detect changes in the concentration of an attractant or repellent and initiate a signaling cascade to control twitching motility.
evidence: Based on homology to flagella MCPs

claim: The ΔpilJ mutant exhibited low twitching motility.
source: In the macroscopic assay, the ΔpilJ mutant exhibited low twitching motility, as previously described (Darzins, 1994) and responded to S. aureus supernatant to a similar degree as the ΔpilA mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by macroscopic twitching assay and citation

claim: ΔpilJ phenocopied the behavior of WT P. aeruginosa in the presence of S. aureus during live-imaging.
source: However, examination by live-imaging revealed that ΔpilJ remained capable of performing surface motility and phenocopied the behavior of WT P. aeruginosa in the presence of S. aureus; moving as single-cells and with preferred directionality towards S. aureus (Figure 6A), suggesting that PilJ is not necessary for exploratory motility.
evidence: Supported by live-imaging observations

claim: PilJ is not necessary for exploratory motility.
source: However, examination by live-imaging revealed that ΔpilJ remained capable of performing surface motility and phenocopied the behavior of WT P. aeruginosa in the presence of S. aureus; moving as single-cells and with preferred directionality towards S. aureus (Figure 6A), suggesting that PilJ is not necessary for exploratory motility.
evidence: Inferred from retention of exploratory motility in ΔpilJ mutant

claim: A ΔpilG mutant is non-motile in a macroscopic sub-surface inoculation assay.
source: Prior work demonstrates that while a ΔpilG mutant is non-motile in a macroscopic sub-surface inoculation assay (as previously described, Bertrand et al., 2010), in a microfluidic assay, individual surface attached P. aeruginosa cells were capable of performing twitching motility on a single-cell level; yet, they were unable to respond to a chemotactic gradient (Oliveira et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: In a microfluidic assay, individual ΔpilG P. aeruginosa cells were capable of performing twitching motility on a single-cell level but were unable to respond to a chemotactic gradient.
source: Prior work demonstrates that while a ΔpilG mutant is non-motile in a macroscopic sub-surface inoculation assay (as previously described, Bertrand et al., 2010), in a microfluidic assay, individual surface attached P. aeruginosa cells were capable of performing twitching motility on a single-cell level; yet, they were unable to respond to a chemotactic gradient (Oliveira et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: ΔpilG phenocopied the ΔpilA mutant in the macroscopic assay and was unable to generate twitching motility.
source: Similar to ΔpilJ we found that ΔpilG phenocopied the ΔpilA mutant in the macroscopic assay and was unable to generate twitching motility (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by macroscopic twitching assay

claim: ΔpilG was diminished in its capacity to increase motility in response to S. aureus during live-imaging.
source: However, during live-imaging, in comparison to ΔpilJ, ΔpilG was diminished in its capacity to increase motility in response to S. aureus (Figure 6B for PA14 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 for PAO1, see discussion).
evidence: Supported by live-imaging observations

claim: When a sufficient number of S. aureus cells were present, ΔpilG would eventually respond to the presence of S. aureus.
source: Interestingly, we did note that in a few circumstances (3 of 9 videos), when a sufficient number of S. aureus cells were present (five or more founding cells per field of view) ΔpilG would eventually respond to the presence of S. aureus (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by live-imaging observations under specific conditions

claim: The ΔpilG mutant displayed a diminished response to S. aureus in comparison to WT P. aeruginosa when imaged simultaneously.
source: Here the ΔpilG mutant displayed a diminished response to S. aureus in comparison to WT P. aeruginosa (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by simultaneous imaging of WT and ΔpilG

claim: A ΔpilG mutant is capable of performing TFP-mediated motility but has a diminished response to chemotactic signals.
source: These data support the previous observations suggesting that a ΔpilG mutant is capable of performing TFP-mediated motility, but has a diminished response to chemotactic signals (Oliveira et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by current observations and citation to previous study

claim: Phenotypic loss of twitching motility in monoculture is often observed in chronic P. aeruginosa isolates from CF patients.
source: Phenotypic loss of twitching motility in monoculture is often observed in chronic P. aeruginosa isolates from CF patients (Mayer-Hamblett et al., 2014), thus it was not surprising that two of the four isolates examined exhibited no detectable twitching motility in the absence of S. aureus.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Two of the four CF P. aeruginosa isolates examined exhibited no detectable twitching motility in the absence of S. aureus.
source: Phenotypic loss of twitching motility in monoculture is often observed in chronic P. aeruginosa isolates from CF patients (Mayer-Hamblett et al., 2014), thus it was not surprising that two of the four isolates examined exhibited no detectable twitching motility in the absence of S. aureus.
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assays with CF isolates

claim: Each CF P. aeruginosa isolate was able to respond to S. aureus supernatant, although to varying degrees.
source: Nonetheless, each P. aeruginosa isolate was able to respond to S. aureus supernatant, although to varying degrees (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assays with CF isolates

claim: Even mucoid P. aeruginosa isolates exhibited at least a two-fold increase in motility in the presence of S. aureus supernatant, above medium alone.
source: Importantly, even mucoid P. aeruginosa isolates (CFPBPA38, 43, 37), exhibited at least a two-fold increase in motility in the presence of S. aureus supernatant, above medium alone.
evidence: Supported by quantitative motility measurements

claim: Supernatant derived from two out of three clinical CF S. aureus isolates was capable of inducing motility of the WT P. aeruginosa laboratory strain.
source: Supernatant derived from two out of three clinical CF S. aureus isolates (each from different patients) was capable of inducing motility of the WT P. aeruginosa laboratory strain, to an extent not significantly different from that previously observed with WT S. aureus (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assays with CF S. aureus isolates

claim: CFBRSA48 was unable to induce P. aeruginosa motility due to reduced activity of the Agr quorum sensing system.
source: Since we previously observed Agr was necessary for S. aureus to promote motility, we hypothesized that CFBRSA48 was unable to induce P. aeruginosa due to reduced activity of the Agr quorum sensing system – an adaptation previously reported for S. aureus CF isolates (Nair et al., 2011; Goerke and Wolz, 2010).
evidence: Hypothesis based on previous observations and citations

claim: Reduced Agr activity is an adaptation previously reported for S. aureus CF isolates.
source: Since we previously observed Agr was necessary for S. aureus to promote motility, we hypothesized that CFBRSA48 was unable to induce P. aeruginosa due to reduced activity of the Agr quorum sensing system – an adaptation previously reported for S. aureus CF isolates (Nair et al., 2011; Goerke and Wolz, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: All three clinical CF S. aureus isolates maintain WT levels of hemolysis.
source: However, all three clinical isolates maintain WT levels of hemolysis, suggesting Agr is active in these strains and an unknown mechanism accounts for reduced activity towards S. aureus in CFBRSA isolate 48 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by hemolysis assay on blood agar

claim: Agr is active in the three clinical CF S. aureus isolates tested.
source: However, all three clinical isolates maintain WT levels of hemolysis, suggesting Agr is active in these strains and an unknown mechanism accounts for reduced activity towards S. aureus in CFBRSA isolate 48 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from maintenance of hemolysis, which is Agr-regulated

claim: An unknown mechanism accounts for reduced activity in CFBRSA isolate 48.
source: However, all three clinical isolates maintain WT levels of hemolysis, suggesting Agr is active in these strains and an unknown mechanism accounts for reduced activity towards S. aureus in CFBRSA isolate 48 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from inability to explain reduced activity by Agr deficiency

claim: One of two B. cepacia isolates tested enhanced P. aeruginosa motility to a similar degree as S. aureus.
source: We observed that one of two B. cepacia isolates tested enhanced P. aeruginosa motility to a similar degree as S. aureus, while none of those tested from H. influenzae or A. xylosoxidans significantly increased motility under these conditions (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assays with CF pathogen isolates

claim: None of the H. influenzae or A. xylosoxidans isolates tested significantly increased P. aeruginosa motility.
source: We observed that one of two B. cepacia isolates tested enhanced P. aeruginosa motility to a similar degree as S. aureus, while none of those tested from H. influenzae or A. xylosoxidans significantly increased motility under these conditions (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assays with CF pathogen isolates

claim: P. aeruginosa showed a significant increase in motility in response to each non-CF organism tested (B. subtilis, E. coli, and S. Typhimurium).
source: While the amount of P. aeruginosa motility observed varied between species and laboratory strains utilized, we observed a significant increase in P. aeruginosa motility in response to each organism tested, demonstrating that P. aeruginosa responds to a variety of bacterial species (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assays with non-CF organisms

claim: P. aeruginosa responds to a variety of bacterial species.
source: While the amount of P. aeruginosa motility observed varied between species and laboratory strains utilized, we observed a significant increase in P. aeruginosa motility in response to each organism tested, demonstrating that P. aeruginosa responds to a variety of bacterial species (Figure 7D).
evidence: Demonstrated by positive responses to multiple bacterial species

claim: Heat treatment did not influence S. aureus supernatant motility-inducing activity.
source: Heat treatment did not influence supernatant motility-inducing activity.
evidence: Supported by biochemical analysis comparing heat-treated and untreated supernatant

claim: Protease treatment of the supernatant, with either proteinase k or trypsin, almost entirely eliminated activity.
source: However, protease treatment of the supernatant, with either proteinase k or trypsin, almost entirely eliminated activity (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by biochemical analysis with protease treatment

claim: The active factors in S. aureus supernatant are heat-stable proteins.
source: These data suggest that the active factors are heat-stable proteins.
evidence: Inferred from heat stability and protease sensitivity

claim: The active factors were soluble in the aqueous fraction following hydrophobic extraction.
source: Supporting this conclusion, we also found that the active factors were soluble in the aqueous fraction following hydrophobic extraction (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by biochemical fractionation experiment

claim: The S. aureus factors responsible for promoting P. aeruginosa surface motility are proteinaceous in nature, but the activity is insensitive to denaturation by heat.
source: These data suggest the S. aureus factors responsible for promoting P. aeruginosa surface motility are proteinaceous in nature, but the activity is insensitive to denaturation by heat.
evidence: Inferred from protease sensitivity and heat stability

claim: S. aureus produces heat-stable, Agr-regulated proteins and/or peptides that promote P. aeruginosa motility.
source: Together our biochemical and genetic evidence predict that heat-stable, Agr-regulated proteins and/or peptides promote P. aeruginosa motility.
evidence: Inferred from combination of biochemical and genetic data

claim: S. aureus PSMs are amphipathic, multifunctional peptides that lyse many human cell types, are pro-inflammatory and chemoattractant to neutrophils, and influence S. aureus biofilm morphology and dispersal.
source: PSMs are amphipathic, multifunctional peptides that lyse many human cell types, are pro-inflammatory and chemoattractant to neutrophils, and influence S. aureus biofilm morphology and dispersal (Cheung et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review

claim: S. aureus produces five α-peptides (PSMα1–4 and δ-toxin) and two β-peptides (PSMβ1 and 2).
source: S. aureus produces five α-peptides (PSMα1–4 and δ-toxin) and two β-peptides (PSMβ1 and 2).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of S. aureus PSMs

claim: Supernatant derived from the Δpsmαβδ mutant showed a significantly reduced ability to promote P. aeruginosa motility in comparison to WT.
source: Supernatant derived from the Δpsmαβδ mutant showed a significantly reduced ability to promote P. aeruginosa motility in comparison to WT; however, the activity remained higher than ΔagrBDCA, suggesting one or more additional unidentified S. aureus factors also promote P. aeruginosa motility (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by twitching motility assay with PSM mutant supernatant

claim: One or more additional unidentified S. aureus factors also promote P. aeruginosa motility.
source: Supernatant derived from the Δpsmαβδ mutant showed a significantly reduced ability to promote P. aeruginosa motility in comparison to WT; however, the activity remained higher than ΔagrBDCA, suggesting one or more additional unidentified S. aureus factors also promote P. aeruginosa motility (Figure 8C).
evidence: Inferred from residual activity in Δpsmαβδ mutant above ΔagrBDCA

claim: P. aeruginosa can respond to secreted products from S. aureus and more broadly to a range of model bacteria and CF pathogens, both Gram-positive and negative.
source: Our data thus far reveal that P. aeruginosa can not only respond to secreted products from S. aureus, but also more broadly to a range of model bacteria and CF pathogens, both Gram-positive and negative.
evidence: Supported by experiments with multiple bacterial species

claim: S. aureus PSMs contribute to the ability of S. aureus to induce surface motility in P. aeruginosa, but do not fully account for the observed phenotype.
source: This insight led to the determination that S. aureus PSMs contribute to the ability of S. aureus to induce surface motility in P. aeruginosa, but do not fully account for the observed phenotype, suggesting that additional unidentified factors are necessary.
evidence: Supported by partial reduction in activity with PSM mutant

claim: S. aureus may produce Agr-independent factors that influence P. aeruginosa motility.
source: Moreover, S. aureus may also produce Agr-independent factors that influence P. aeruginosa motility, given that an Agr-deficient strain is unable to induce motility in the macroscopic sub-surface inoculation motility assay or directional motility on either the macroscopic or single-cell level, but remains capable of increasing single-cell motility during live-imaging.
evidence: Inferred from retention of some activity in Agr mutant during live-imaging

claim: Separate factors may be required for initiating single-cell motility and directional motion.
source: Thus, it is formally possible that separate factors are required for initiating single-cell motility and directional motion.
evidence: Speculated based on differential effects of Agr mutant in different assays

claim: P. aeruginosa cells may actively avoid Agr-deficient S. aureus.
source: Live-imaging also suggests that P. aeruginosa cells may actively avoid Agr-deficient S. aureus, raising the possibility that the Agr system negatively regulates a secreted factor that is unfavorable for P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Based on observation of cell trajectories away from ΔagrBDCA

claim: The Agr system may negatively regulate a secreted factor that is unfavorable for P. aeruginosa.
source: Live-imaging also suggests that P. aeruginosa cells may actively avoid Agr-deficient S. aureus, raising the possibility that the Agr system negatively regulates a secreted factor that is unfavorable for P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Speculated based on avoidance behavior towards ΔagrBDCA

claim: PSMs are amphipathic peptides that are able to reduce interfacial tension (IFT).
source: PSMs are amphipathic peptides that are able to reduce interfacial tension (IFT), that is, the cohesive or excess energy between molecules at an interface.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PSM properties

claim: Surfactants play an essential role in flagella-mediated bacterial surface motility (swarming).
source: While such surfactants have been extensively characterized to play an essential role in flagella-mediated bacterial surface motility, referred to as swarming (Kearns, 2010), their role in TFP-mediated motility is not well described.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review

claim: The role of surfactants in TFP-mediated motility is not well described.
source: While such surfactants have been extensively characterized to play an essential role in flagella-mediated bacterial surface motility, referred to as swarming (Kearns, 2010), their role in TFP-mediated motility is not well described.
evidence: Based on assessment of current literature

claim: TFP generate bacterial movement on surfaces through polymerization and extension of pilus fibers, followed by pilus retraction, which pulls the cell body forward.
source: TFP generate bacterial movement on surfaces though polymerization and extension of pilus fibers, followed by pilus retraction, which pulls the cell body forward.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TFP mechanism

claim: Reduced IFT between the cell body and the surface may reduce drag on the cell body and reduce the force necessary to retract the pilus.
source: Reduced IFT between the cell body and the surface, without affecting interaction between the pilus tip and the surface, may reduce drag on the cell body and reduce the force necessary to retract the pilus.
evidence: Speculated mechanism based on surfactant properties

claim: TFP-mediated motility is most often described as a behavior where cells are primarily motile only in large groups.
source: TFP-mediated motility is most often described as a behavior where cells are primarily motile only in large groups.
evidence: Based on established descriptions in the literature

claim: The behaviors for WT P. aeruginosa in monoculture are consistent with previous descriptions of twitching motility.
source: The behaviors for WT P. aeruginosa in monoculture observed here are consistent with previous descriptions of twitching motility, including the movement of cells in rafts, preferentially aligned along their long axis, and group tendril formation at the edges of the expanding community (Burrows, 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison to cited previous descriptions

claim: PSMs may reduce the IFT between neighboring P. aeruginosa cells, disrupting collective movement within rafts.
source: Perhaps PSMs also reduce the IFT between neighboring P. aeruginosa cells, disrupting collective movement within rafts.
evidence: Speculated mechanism for transition to single-cell motility

claim: PSMs are known to promote S. aureus spreading on wet surfaces, in particular PSMα3 and δ-toxin, which possess high surfactant activity and low hydrophobicity.
source: PSMs are known to promote S. aureus spreading on wet surfaces, in particular PSMα3 and δ-toxin, which possess high surfactant activity and low hydrophobicity (Tsompanidou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: B. subtilis strain 3610 induced P. aeruginosa motility similar to S. aureus.
source: 3610 induced P. aeruginosa motility similar to S. aureus.
evidence: Supported by motility assay data

claim: B. subtilis strain PY79 did not induce P. aeruginosa motility and is deficient in surfactant production.
source: In comparison to PY79, which did not induce motility and is deficient in surfactant production, 3610 is an undomesticated strain that secretes a potent lipopeptide surfactant, called surfactin (Kearns and Losick, 2003).
evidence: Supported by motility assay data and citation

claim: B. subtilis strain 3610 is an undomesticated strain that secretes a potent lipopeptide surfactant, called surfactin.
source: In comparison to PY79, which did not induce motility and is deficient in surfactant production, 3610 is an undomesticated strain that secretes a potent lipopeptide surfactant, called surfactin (Kearns and Losick, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The different levels of surfactin may account for the differential ability of B. subtilis strains to promote P. aeruginosa motility.
source: Thus, it is interesting to speculate that the different levels of surfactin account for the differential ability of these B. subtilis strains to promote P. aeruginosa motility.
evidence: Speculated based on correlation between surfactin production and motility induction

claim: PSMs can form small transient pores in lipid membranes resulting in cell lysis of eukaryotic and some prokaryotic cells.
source: PSMs can also form small transient pores in lipid membranes resulting in cell lysis of eukaryotic and some prokaryotic cells (Cheung et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review

claim: Interactions of PSMs with the P. aeruginosa outer membrane may influence P. aeruginosa surface motility, independent of reduced IFT at the surface.
source: Thus, it is possible that interactions of PSMs with the P. aeruginosa outer membrane influence P. aeruginosa surface motility, independent of reduced IFT at the surface.
evidence: Speculated alternative mechanism based on PSM properties

claim: Surfactin has been shown to influence B. subtilis quorum sensing and biofilm formation through the formation of membrane pores, resulting in potassium leakage.
source: For example, surfactin has been shown to influence B. subtilis quorum sensing and biofilm formation through the formation of membrane pores, resulting in potassium leakage. The resulting low cellular potassium activates the protein kinase, KinC, which regulates biofilm formation (López et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Low cellular potassium activates the protein kinase, KinC, which regulates biofilm formation in B. subtilis.
source: For example, surfactin has been shown to influence B. subtilis quorum sensing and biofilm formation through the formation of membrane pores, resulting in potassium leakage. The resulting low cellular potassium activates the protein kinase, KinC, which regulates biofilm formation (López et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: P. aeruginosa was shown to direct motility on agar surfaces up a gradient of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE).
source: In initial studies of TFP-mediated chemotaxis, P. aeruginosa was shown to direct motility on agar surfaces up a gradient of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) (Kearns et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: A ΔpilJ mutant did not exhibit preferential movement up a PE gradient.
source: While a ΔpilJ mutant did not exhibit preferential movement up a PE gradient, the lack of twitching motility in this mutant prohibited interpretation of a role for PilJ.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The lack of twitching motility in the ΔpilJ mutant prohibited interpretation of a role for PilJ in chemotaxis.
source: While a ΔpilJ mutant did not exhibit preferential movement up a PE gradient, the lack of twitching motility in this mutant prohibited interpretation of a role for PilJ.
evidence: Based on limitation of previous experimental approach

claim: Twitching cells move by pulling themselves along by pili clustered at one pole.
source: Twitching cells move by pulling themselves along by pili clustered at one pole.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of twitching motility mechanism

claim: Cells can reverse direction by extending the pili from the opposite pole, changing the direction of movement along the long axis.
source: Cells can reverse direction by extending the pili from the opposite pole, changing the direction of movement along the long axis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of twitching motility mechanism

claim: Reversals have been suggested to be important for P. aeruginosa to direct movement up a chemotactic gradient while on a surface.
source: These reversals have recently been suggested to be important for P. aeruginosa to direct movement up a chemotactic gradient while on a surface (Oliveira et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In a ΔpilG mutant, cells performed fewer reversals in comparison to WT in response to a chemotactic gradient and were unable to bias the directionality of their movement.
source: In a ΔpilG mutant (the response regulator for pilus extension), cells were observed to perform fewer reversals in comparison to WT in response to a chemotactic gradient and thus were unable to bias the directionality of their movement.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Both ΔpilJ and ΔpilG mutants have been previously reported to be deficient in producing traditional twitch rings in the macroscopic sub-surface inoculation assay.
source: Both ΔpilJ and ΔpilG mutants have been previously reported to be deficient in producing traditional twitch rings in the macroscopic sub-surface inoculation assay (Luo et al., 2015; Bertrand et al., 2010; Darzins, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The collective movements of ΔpilJ and ΔpilG mutants as measured in bulk assays may not be reflected on the single-cell level.
source: Our observations here for PilJ and PilG, combined with those from Oliveira et al. suggest the collective movements of these mutants as measured in bulk assays may not be reflected on the single-cell level.
evidence: Inferred from discrepancy between bulk and single-cell observations

claim: M. xanthus coordinates a cooperative, density-dependent feeding behavior, resulting in propulsion of the cells rapidly through the colony of prey, leading to prey lysis, and nutrient acquisition.
source: M. xanthus coordinates a cooperative, density-dependent feeding behavior, resulting in propulsion of the cells rapidly through the colony of prey, leading to prey lysis, and nutrient acquisition.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of M. xanthus predatory behavior

claim: When M. xanthus contacts prey cells, pili-dependent reversals are stimulated, which keeps the cells 'trapped' near the prey colony.
source: When M. xanthus contacts prey cells, pili-dependent reversals are stimulated, which keeps the cells 'trapped' near the prey colony, promoting contact-dependent prey killing and increased local concentration of antimicrobials (Muñoz-Dorado et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review

claim: Pili-dependent reversals in M. xanthus promote contact-dependent prey killing and increased local concentration of antimicrobials.
source: When M. xanthus contacts prey cells, pili-dependent reversals are stimulated, which keeps the cells 'trapped' near the prey colony, promoting contact-dependent prey killing and increased local concentration of antimicrobials (Muñoz-Dorado et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review

claim: P. aeruginosa produces an arsenal of secreted antimicrobials shown to inhibit the growth of S. aureus.
source: P. aeruginosa produces an arsenal of secreted antimicrobials shown to inhibit the growth of S. aureus, yet these secreted factors alone are insufficient for cellular lysis (Limoli et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: P. aeruginosa secreted factors alone are insufficient for S. aureus cellular lysis.
source: P. aeruginosa produces an arsenal of secreted antimicrobials shown to inhibit the growth of S. aureus, yet these secreted factors alone are insufficient for cellular lysis (Limoli et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The exploratory motility behaviors may function to synergistically increase cellular contacts necessary to kill S. aureus by a contact-dependent mechanism and/or to locally increase the concentration of secreted products.
source: Thus, it is interesting to speculate that these behaviors function to synergistically increase cellular contacts necessary to kill S. aureus by a contact-dependent mechanism and/or to locally increase the concentration of secreted products.
evidence: Speculated based on analogy to M. xanthus and known P. aeruginosa antimicrobial properties
